issues.legal_issue: An elected local official’s failure to call a required meeting does not, without more, establish misconduct warranting removal.
material_facts: The elected council president admitted that an ordinary council meeting had not been called for a three-month period.
The president furnished an explanation for the omission, but the competent authority did not consider it.
There was no finding that the president intentionally avoided a meeting or that any urgent or important work was prevented by the omission.
The statutory scheme provided other means by which a meeting could be called if the president failed to do so.
issues.conclusion: The admitted failure to call the meeting, without evidence of intentional misconduct or resulting harm, did not warrant removal; the explanation should have been considered.
issues.legal_principle: Misconduct must be assessed in context and ordinarily involves wrongful, forbidden or wilful conduct; a mere error of judgment, carelessness or negligence is not enough, though negligence may amount to misconduct in exceptional circumstances. Misconduct must also be assessed for its effect on the public interest. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Ram Singh Ex. Constable, Disciplinary Authority-cum-Regional Manager v. Nikunja Bihari Patnaik, Government of A.P. v. P. Posetty, M.M. Malhotra v. Union of India, Baldev Singh Gandhi v. State of Punjab, and General Manager, Appellate Authority, Bank of India v. Mohd. Nizamuddin. The meeting requirement and alternative procedures were set out in Section 81 of the Maharashtra Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats and Industrial Townships Act, 1965.

rule.if: elected_official_removal_case and meeting_omitted and reasonable_explanation_furnished and not intentional_avoidance_proved and not resulting_public_harm_proved

predicates.elected_official_removal_case: A proceeding seeks to remove an elected local official for alleged misconduct.
predicates.meeting_omitted: The elected official failed to call a meeting required for the body's ordinary business.
predicates.reasonable_explanation_furnished: The official gave an explanation for failing to call the meeting.
predicates.intentional_avoidance_proved: Evidence established that the official deliberately failed to call the meeting to avoid a matter or demand.
predicates.resulting_public_harm_proved: Evidence established that the failure prevented urgent or important public business.

issues.definition: When an elected local official in a removal proceeding failed to call a required meeting but gave an explanation, and neither deliberate avoidance nor resulting public harm was proved, the omission alone does not warrant removal.

issues.legal_issue: An elected official cannot be held individually responsible for a contract accepted by the council as a collective decision rather than by the official alone.
material_facts: The tenders for pipeline work were considered after technical review and recommendations by the chief officer and junior engineer, together with the president’s signature.
The council itself passed a resolution accepting the tenders after deliberation.
The acceptance was not a contract awarded by the president alone or a later ratification of a contract independently awarded by the president.
issues.conclusion: The charges relating to acceptance of the tenders could not be proved against the president individually.
issues.legal_principle: Individual responsibility for misconduct must be supported by the evidence; a collective decision of the council cannot, on the facts here, be treated as the president’s individual decision. Section 55B of the Maharashtra Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats and Industrial Townships Act, 1965 concerns disqualification for proved misconduct in the discharge of official duties.

rule.if: elected_official_removal_case and contract_acceptance_considered_by_council and council_collectively_approved_contract and official_did_not_individually_award_contract

predicates.elected_official_removal_case: A proceeding seeks to remove or disqualify an elected local official for alleged misconduct.
predicates.contract_acceptance_considered_by_counci: The council considered the contract after relevant officials reviewed and recommended it.
predicates.council_collectively_approved_contract: The council passed a collective resolution accepting the contract.
predicates.official_did_not_individually_award_cont: The official did not independently award the contract or later seek ratification of a contract awarded by the official alone.

issues.definition: If a contract was reviewed and approved by the council collectively and was not awarded by the official alone, the official is not individually responsible for that collective decision.

issues.legal_issue: Removal of an elected local official for misconduct requires strict adherence to the prescribed procedure, a fair opportunity to defend, and a reasoned decision addressing the allegations and the official’s explanation.
material_facts: The competent authority imposed removal and a further period of disqualification on an elected council president.

The authority’s order did not address the president’s explanation concerning the meeting or the council’s role in accepting the tenders, and it gave no reasons explaining its conclusions on those matters.
The High Court upheld the order without addressing the president’s material grievances or giving reasons for upholding the findings.
The removal order carried serious consequences for the elected official and the constituency he represented.
issues.conclusion: The removal and disqualification orders could not stand; the appeal was allowed and both the authority’s order and the High Court judgment were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Removal of an elected representative for proved misconduct is quasi-judicial in nature and requires strict compliance with statutory safeguards and natural justice, including a fair opportunity to defend and a decision showing application of mind to the allegations and explanation. Serious consequences require particular care. Administrative and quasi-judicial decisions must give reasons sufficient to show application of mind and permit effective review. The Court relied on Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution; Sections 55A and 55B of the Maharashtra Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats and Industrial Townships Act, 1965; State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh; G. Sadanandan v. State of Kerala; Indian National Congress (I) v. Institute of Social Welfare; Bachhitar Singh v. State of Punjab; Union of India v. H.C. Goel; Tarlochan Dev Sharma v. State of Punjab; Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P.; S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India; and Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. L.K. Ratna.

rule.if: elected_official_removal_case and serious_removal_consequences and not fair_opportunity_provided or elected_official_removal_case and serious_removal_consequences and not material_explanation_considered or elected_official_removal_case and serious_removal_consequences and not reasons_recorded

predicates.elected_official_removal_case: A proceeding concerns removal or disqualification of an elected local official for alleged misconduct.
predicates.serious_removal_consequences: The decision removes the official from elected office or imposes a further disqualification.
predicates.fair_opportunity_provided: The official was given a fair opportunity to answer the allegations and material grounds relied on.
predicates.material_explanation_considered: The decision-maker considered the official’s material explanation and addressed it in reaching the decision.
predicates.reasons_recorded: The decision gives reasons showing how the evidence and explanation support its conclusions.

issues.definition: When a decision imposing serious consequences on an elected official is made without a fair opportunity, consideration of the material explanation, or recorded reasons, the removal decision cannot stand.

issues.legal_issue: A complainant who has no legal injury or legally protected interest is not entitled to participate as an adversarial party in proceedings to remove an elected official.
material_facts: The complainant was a former council president and sitting councillor who was a political rival of the elected official.
The complainant did not establish that a legal right or legally protected interest of his had been injured or threatened.
The complaint could nevertheless be used as material to collect evidence and ascertain the truth.
issues.conclusion: The complainant could not claim the status of an adversarial party and could at most provide material or evidence for the inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: A person must establish a legal injury or a legally protected interest to be heard as an aggrieved party; a fanciful grievance, remote interest or general public-interest claim is insufficient. The Court relied on Adi Pherozshah Gandhi v. H.M. Seervai, Jasbhai Motibhai Desai v. Roshan Kumar, Maharaj Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Ghulam Qadir v. Special Tribunal, and Kabushiki Kaisha Toshiba v. Tosiba Appliances Company.

predicates.official_removal_proceeding: A proceeding is brought to remove or disqualify an elected official.
predicates.complainant_lacks_legal_injury: The complainant has not shown that the challenged conduct injured or threatens a legal right belonging to the complainant.
predicates.complainant_lacks_legally_protected_inte: The complainant has not shown a legally protected interest entitling the complainant to participate as a party.

issues.definition: In a proceeding to remove an elected official, a complainant who shows neither personal legal injury nor a legally protected interest cannot participate as an adversarial party.

issues.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference when a public authority fails to produce a record it was directed to produce for examination of a material procedural allegation.
material_facts: The elected official alleged that the hearing had been adjourned to give him an opportunity to answer new grounds raised by the complainant.
The Supreme Court directed the State to produce the original record so the allegation could be examined.
The State neither produced the record nor applied for an extension of time.
issues.conclusion: The Court drew an adverse inference against the State because the directed record was not produced.
issues.legal_principle: Where a party fails to produce material evidence or a record that the Court has directed it to produce, the Court may draw an adverse inference in the circumstances. The judgment applied that principle to the State’s failure to produce the original record after the Court’s direction.

predicates.court_directed_record_production: The court directed an authority to produce a record.
predicates.record_material_to_procedural_allegation: The record could assist the court in examining a material allegation about the fairness or conduct of the proceedings.
predicates.authority_failed_to_produce_record: The authority did not produce the directed record or obtain an extension to do so.

issues.definition: If a court directs an authority to produce a record material to a procedural allegation and the authority fails to produce it, an adverse inference may be drawn against the authority.
